Adult Viola (Loricariichthys anus) attain a maximum total length of 46 cm [Li = 46 cm], placing them among the larger members of the Loricariinae subfamily in the Paraná River basin. Field surveys conducted in the middle Paraná floodplain indicate that reproductive maturity, signaled by the onset of gonadal recrudescence, is typically reached at a total length of 21 cm [Lp = 21 cm]. This length threshold corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 68.7 grams [Wwp = 68.7 grams], a value derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship for this loricariid. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic body mass achieved by fully grown adults, reaches 879.6 grams [Wwi = 879.6 grams], highlighting the considerable somatic growth that occurs between maturation and senescence. This pronounced post-maturation growth is characteristic of iteroparous teleosts that continue to allocate resources to somatic increase well after the onset of breeding activity.

Embryonic and early larval development in Viola proceed rapidly under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Yolk-sac larvae emerge from the demersal, adhesive eggs following an incubation period of approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days], a developmental duration that is consistent with values reported for the congeneric Loricariichthys platymetopon at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At the moment of chorion rupture, the newly emerged prolarvae possess a wet weight of roughly 0.0024 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0024 grams], reflecting the modest size of the fertilized ovum, which is based on an egg diameter of 1.67 mm. This small birth mass necessitates a brief endotrophic phase during which the larva relies entirely on its yolk reserves before the mouth opens and the trophic switch to exogenous feeding begins, typically within a few days of emergence.

Based on reproductive parameters estimated from the closely related species Loricariichthys platymetopon, the maximum annual reproductive output of Viola can be characterized in terms of fecundity and spawning frequency. At a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], gravid females produce approximately 880 oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 880 oocytes per spawning event], a batch fecundity that reflects the species' relatively high relative fecundity of 7.6 oocytes per gram of body mass. Reproductive activity is concentrated within the austral summer months, during which females may complete as many as 7.6 spawning events per year [F_R_i = 7.6 spawning events per year], a frequency that is tightly linked to the warm thermal regime prevalent in the floodplain during the breeding season. The combination of moderate batch fecundity and elevated spawning frequency yields a substantial annual reproductive investment.

At the same thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], longevity records for Viola, derived from mark-recapture studies in the Paraná River system, indicate that individuals can survive for up to 9 years [am = up to 9 years] under natural conditions. This maximum lifespan of 9 years is notable among neotropical loricariids, as it aligns with a relatively slow life-history pace characterized by delayed maturity and extended reproductive tenure. The species' lifespan appears to be further modulated by thermal conditions, as sustained temperatures of 25 °C appear to optimize both somatic growth and reproductive output without accelerating senescence. Older individuals, particularly those exceeding 7 years of age, exhibit a gradual decline in body condition and a reduction in spawning frequency, consistent with the onset of reproductive senescence.

Comparative analysis of life-history traits across Loricariichthys species reveals that Viola occupies an intermediate position along the slow-fast continuum. For instance, the total length at puberty recorded for Viola represents roughly 46 percent of its ultimate total length, a maturation schedule that is slower than that of the smaller congener Loricariichthys castaneus but faster than that of the larger-bodied Loricariichthys labialis. The habitat preferences of Viola, which include lentic backwaters and slow-flowing channels with abundant submerged vegetation, are closely tied to its reproductive ecology. Under the stable thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the development of demersal eggs proceeds efficiently, and the incubation period of approximately 8 days ensures that yolk-sac larvae emerge during the warm summer months when zooplankton prey is abundant for first-feeding exotrophic larvae. Ongoing studies are examining how projected shifts in floodplain hydrology and temperature may affect the species' growth trajectories and population dynamics.
